assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Cohesion
items.clue: The attraction between molecules of the same substance.

items.label: Viscosity
items.clue: The resistance of a fluid to flow, due to friction between its moving layers.

items.label: Adhesion
items.clue: The attraction between water molecules and molecules of a different substance.

items.label: Specific heat capacity
items.clue: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K (1 °C).

questions.stem: Water is described as the medium for life. What does this mean?

options.text: Most of the processes of life take place in aqueous solution.
Water is inert packing between the working parts of a cell.
Every substance that a cell uses must be dissolved in water.
Life processes occur in water only in aquatic organisms.

questions.explanation: The first cells originated in water, and water remains the medium in which most processes of life occur: metabolic reactions happen in the aqueous cytoplasm and substances are transported dissolved in water.

questions.stem: Why is each covalent bond between oxygen and hydrogen in a water molecule polar?

options.text: Each hydrogen atom gives up its electron completely to the oxygen atom.
The shared electrons are drawn more strongly towards the oxygen atom.
It is a hydrogen bond, and hydrogen bonds are polar by their nature.
Oxygen and hydrogen atoms behave as opposite magnetic poles.

questions.explanation: Oxygen attracts the shared electron pair more strongly than hydrogen does, so the electrons are shared unequally: oxygen becomes δ− and each hydrogen δ+. This unequal sharing is what makes the bond polar.

questions.stem: Transpiration puts the column of water in a xylem vessel under tension. Why does the column not break as it is pulled upwards?

options.text: Root pressure pushes the column upwards from below.
Capillary action lifts the water inside the narrow vessel.
Hydrogen bonds within each molecule resist the pull.
Hydrogen bonds hold the molecules to each other.

questions.explanation: Cohesion due to hydrogen bonding keeps the water molecules attached to one another, so the tension created by evaporation in the leaves is transmitted down the whole column and water is drawn up without the column separating.

questions.stem: Water rises through the narrow spaces between soil particles, against gravity. Which explanation of this movement is correct?

options.text: Cohesion between the water and the soil particles draws the water upwards.
Water adheres to the polar or charged surfaces of the soil particles.
Water adheres to any solid surface, whatever the surface is made of.
Air pressure in the soil pushes the water up into the spaces.

questions.explanation: Soil particle surfaces are polar or charged, so water molecules are attracted to them (adhesion). Together with cohesion between water molecules, this pulls water through the narrow spaces: capillary action.

questions.stem: Why do so many different substances dissolve in water?

options.text: Water splits every solute into positive and negative ions.
Water breaks the covalent bonds within the solute molecules.
Water molecules are magnetic and so attract other substances.
Polar water molecules attract polar and charged solutes.

questions.explanation: The δ+ and δ− regions of water molecules are attracted to charged particles and to the polar groups of molecules, so a wide variety of hydrophilic substances dissolve. This is why water is the medium for metabolism and transport.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes a consequence of the physical properties of water for a ringed seal (Pusa hispida)?

options.text: Because it can sink, the water gives its body no support.
It loses heat slowly because water is a poor conductor of heat.
Upthrust from the sea water supports most of its body weight.
The sea stays warm because of water's high specific heat capacity.

questions.explanation: Water is dense, so the upthrust on the seal's body is close to its weight (buoyancy). The seal needs far less skeletal support than a land animal, which receives negligible upthrust from air.

questions.stem: During transpiration, water molecules leave the liquid on the surface of a cell wall and enter the air. Which bonds are broken as each molecule leaves?

options.text: Polar covalent bonds between its oxygen and hydrogen atoms
Hydrogen bonds between the oxygen and hydrogens inside it
Hydrogen bonds between it and neighbouring molecules
Ionic bonds between its oxygen and hydrogen ions

questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonds link the δ+ hydrogens of one molecule to the δ− oxygens of its neighbours. These weak intermolecular bonds must be broken for the molecule to leave the liquid; the covalent bonds inside it are unaffected.

questions.stem: A pond skater rests on a pond. Its legs make small dents in the water surface but do not pass through it. What allows the surface to support the insect?

options.text: Cohesion between surface molecules makes the surface act like an elastic film.
The insect is less dense than water, so upthrust holds it at the surface.
Water adheres to the insect's legs and so holds them up on the surface.
The strong hydrogen bonds at the surface form a rigid, solid-like layer.

questions.explanation: Molecules at the surface are held to their neighbours by hydrogen bonds and resist being separated, so the surface behaves like a stretched film. This surface tension, a consequence of cohesion, lets small animals use the water surface as a habitat.

questions.stem: In a leaf, water evaporates from the cellulose cell walls of spongy mesophyll cells. How does adhesion contribute to water transport?

options.text: It pushes water out of the xylem into the cell walls under root pressure.
It holds water against the waxy cuticle so that less of it evaporates.
It draws water into the cell walls to replace water that evaporates.
It alone lifts water the whole way from the roots up to the leaf.

questions.explanation: Water adheres to the polar cellulose of the cell walls, so as water evaporates it is replaced by water drawn through the walls by capillary action. This pull is transmitted to the xylem, generating the tension that moves water up the plant.

questions.stem: Which statement about the hydrophobic hydrocarbon tails of the phospholipids in a cell membrane is correct?

options.text: Their insolubility in water is what holds the bilayer together as a barrier.
Their insolubility means that they have no function in the membrane.
They are pushed away from water by a repulsive force from water molecules.
They are insoluble because they contain no ions that water can separate.

questions.explanation: Because the tails are non-polar and insoluble, they are excluded from water and cluster together in the centre of the bilayer, with the hydrophilic heads facing the water. The membrane's function depends on the tails being hydrophobic.

questions.stem: A black-throated loon (Gavia arctica) flies through air and dives through water. Which statement about these two fluids is correct?

options.text: Water is far more viscous than air, so it resists the loon's movement much more.
Air has no viscosity, so the loon meets no resistance when it flies.
Water conducts heat more slowly than air, so the loon cools less when diving.
Water stores more heat than air, so the loon is kept warmer while it dives.

questions.explanation: Water's viscosity is about 50 times that of air, so a diving loon meets far greater resistance than a flying one. Animals that move through water benefit from streamlining for this reason.

questions.stem: Glucose is carried dissolved in blood plasma and in phloem sap, and it is broken down by enzymes in the aqueous cytoplasm. Which property of glucose makes this possible?

options.text: It separates into positive and negative ions in water.
Its many hydroxyl (–OH) groups form hydrogen bonds with water.
It is a small molecule, and small molecules dissolve readily.
Water breaks its covalent bonds, splitting it into soluble fragments.

questions.stem: The Moon formed close to Earth and was struck by the same water-bearing asteroids, yet its surface has almost no water today. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: It has no ozone layer to act as a lid that keeps water vapour in.
Its gravity is too weak to hold water vapour, which escapes to space.
It had no volcanoes to release water made from rock in its interior.
It lies outside the Goldilocks zone, so any water froze or boiled off.

questions.explanation: Retention of water depends on gravity strong enough to hold water molecules and on temperatures low enough for water to condense. The Moon's small mass gives it gravity too weak to retain water vapour, so water delivered by asteroids was lost.

questions.stem: Astronomers find a rocky planet orbiting within the Goldilocks zone of its star. Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: Liquid water and living organisms must both exist on the planet's surface.
It orbits at the same distance from its star as Earth does from the Sun.
Any water there, whether ice, liquid or vapour, would support life equally.
Liquid water could exist on its surface, so it is worth investigating.

questions.explanation: The Goldilocks zone is the range of distances at which surface temperatures could allow liquid water. That makes the planet a candidate for the search for life, but the presence of water and of life must be established separately.

questions.stem: Where is most of the water on Earth thought to have come from?

options.text: From hydrogen and oxygen gases that reacted in the early atmosphere
From water formed inside the Earth and released by volcanoes
From water-bearing asteroids that collided with the early Earth
From nowhere: planets in the Goldilocks zone are bound to hold liquid water

questions.explanation: The hypothesis in the guide is that Earth's water is of extraplanetary origin, delivered by water-bearing asteroids that struck the early Earth. Its abundance since then has allowed life to evolve.
